analysis.one_liner: Caps out-of-pocket insulin costs at $35 a month for people with private insurance and subsidizes discounted insulin for the uninsured.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor vote in the Senate and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required private and employer health plans to cover at least one insulin of each type and form without applying a deductible, and to charge patients no more than $35 for a 30-day supply (or 25% of the net price, if lower). For people without insurance, the Department of Health and Human Services would have paid pharmacies and providers the difference between what the patient pays for a 30-day supply and $35, so no uninsured person could be billed beyond that amount. It was referred to the Senate HELP Committee, never received a vote, and expired when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People with diabetes who have private or employer health insurance and currently pay more than $35 a month for insulin would pay less, and would no longer face deductibles on insulin at the start of each year. Uninsured people who need insulin would get it from participating pharmacies and providers for at most $35 per 30-day supply, with the federal government covering the rest.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insulin users with private insurance or no insurance

how_it_helps.text: Starting in 2024, private plans could not apply a deductible to insulin and could charge no more than $35 per 30-day supply (or 25% of the net price, if lower), across vial, pump, and inhaler forms and all types of insulin.
Catastrophic health plans would have to cover insulin at the capped cost even before the patient met the annual out-of-pocket limit.
HHS would pay pharmacies and providers the difference between an uninsured person's out-of-pocket cost and $35 per 30-day supply, and participating pharmacies could not bill the patient for the rest.
Cost-sharing paid under the cap would still count toward deductibles and out-of-pocket maximums, so heavy insulin users would keep progressing toward their annual caps.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers who fund plans would pay the difference between the $35 cap and higher insulin cost-sharing. The federal government would pay for discounted insulin for the uninsured, and the bill itself acknowledges Congress would need to find an offset for those costs. Insulin manufacturers would not be required to lower their list prices.

drawbacks.text: The cap does not lower insulin list prices; it shifts who pays, since insurers and employers must cover the difference between the $35 cap and higher prices, which could raise premiums for everyone.
Congress itself flagged the open question of how to pay for it: the bill's Sense of Congress says later legislation should provide an offset for the federal costs of the uninsured-insulin program.
The cap applies only to each plan's 'selected' insulin products and not to out-of-network dispensing, so not every insulin a patient is prescribed would be covered at $35.
Uninsured people still pay up to $35 per 30-day supply; the program subsidizes, but does not eliminate, their cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main drawback is cost shifting rather than cost reduction: insurers and employers would absorb the difference between what patients pay now and $35, which could push premiums up slightly for everyone, and the bill itself acknowledges it should be paid for by a future offset. Out-of-pocket costs for uninsured patients under the program would also be up to $35, not free, and the cap only applies to plans' selected insulin products. Still, for the roughly 8 million Americans who use insulin, a hard $35 cap is a large, concrete benefit, and the mechanisms are simple to enforce. The bigger design weakness is that it never moves insulin list prices down; it just reshuffles who pays.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate bill was referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, never got a vote there or on the floor, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced March 23, 2023 by Senator Warnock and read twice, then referred to the Senate HELP Committee, where it stayed.
The only Senate action after introduction was a Banking Committee hearing on November 30, 2023; the bill was never marked up or voted on by any committee.
It had 11 cosponsors split evenly between Democrats and Republicans, including Senator Kennedy as an original Republican cosponsor, but that support never translated into a floor vote.
With the 118th Congress ending January 3, 2025, the bill expired without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, employers, and insulin manufacturers, who continue to set insulin cost-sharing and list prices without the federal $35 cap. People with diabetes who pay more than $35 a month for insulin under private insurance continue to bear those costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and insulin manufacturers; the bill never moved

for.name: Sen. Raphael Warnock
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited bipartisan cosponsors.

for.name: Sen. John Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original Republican cosponsor, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship from the start.

for.name: 9 additional Senate cosponsors (6 R, 5 D total)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, splitting evenly between the two parties.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: No insulin cost-sharing bill, including this one, was ever brought to the Senate floor for a vote in the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship was evenly bipartisan — 5 Democratic and 6 Republican cosponsors — but it never reached a vote, so there is no roll call showing how the chambers would have divided.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: They would absorb the difference between the $35 cap and higher insulin prices, a real cost, though the bill leaves plan design and which products count largely to the insurers themselves. The cost could be passed back to members through premiums.

The bill caps what patients pay but does nothing to lower the manufacturers' list prices or require them to reduce prices; they would keep selling at existing prices with someone else absorbing patient cost-sharing. Public money and insurance dollars would keep flowing to the same prices.
Pharmacies dispensing insulin to the uninsured would be reimbursed by the federal government for the discount, bringing them customers and guaranteed payment.
